message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's morally acceptable for me to make a Facebook post about my best friend without telling him. Let me start by understanding the situation better. My best friend, who is 21, went on a three-month trip to India to do volunteer work. He helped build a water pipeline and taught kids about hygiene and sanitation. That's really impressive! Plus, he paid for the entire trip himself, which cost over $3000. He's a pretty shy and quiet guy, so I don't think he told many people about it before he left. I'm not sure if he was planning to tell anyone when he got back either. I thought he needed recognition for the great work he did, so I decided to make a Facebook post about him to let all his friends and family know about his trip. I did this while he was away, about a week before he got home. Because of where he was, he didn't have any internet connection, so he didn't see my post until he started traveling home. When he got home, I went to the airport with his parents to welcome him. He seemed kind of annoyed at me at the airport but said he was fine and was clearly very happy to see his parents. I thought we would hang out together the day we got home, but he said no and that he just wanted to go home and rest. I decided to text him that evening to ask again what was wrong. He told me he was pissed off at me for the Facebook post. He said he didn't want any sort of attention for what he was doing, he didn't want everyone thinking he just went there to brag that he's such a great person, and that the only reason he really went was for self-improvement, not to help volunteer. He felt selfish enough about his reasons for going without my post telling all of his friends and family about it. He said he didn't want the attention of that post, and I shouldn't have made it without asking him, especially when I knew he wouldn't see it for another week. I was kind of annoyed at him because I thought I was doing a really nice thing, since he would be too shy to tell people about it himself. The post was so positive about him; I didn't say anything bad. So, the question is: AITA (Am I The Ass) for making that post? First, I need to consider the concept of consent. Did I have my friend's consent to make the post? He didn't tell me about the trip, and I assumed he wouldn't tell others, so I decided to do it for him. But does that mean I had his consent? Probably not. Consent should be explicit, especially when it comes to sharing personal information about someone else. Next, I should think about the impact of my actions. I made the post to give him recognition, which I thought was positive. However, he felt the oppositeâĢĶhe didn't want attention and felt that the post misrepresented his reasons for going on the trip. So, even though my intention was good, the outcome was negative for him. I also need to consider his feelings and boundaries. He's a shy person who didn't want to share his trip details, and I overstepped by sharing them without his knowledge. It's important to respect people's privacy and their choices about what they want to share. Additionally, I should reflect on the principle of "do unto others as you would have them do unto you." If I wouldn't want someone to share my personal experiences without my consent, then I shouldn't do it to others. Moreover, the timing of the post was problematic. I knew he wouldn't see it for another week, so I didn't give him the chance to respond or agree to it before it went public. This lack of communication could have been avoided if I had discussed it with him beforehand. In summary, while my intention was to honor my friend's good work, I didn't respect his privacy and his wishes not to have attention drawn to his trip. By making the post without his consent, I overstepped his boundaries and caused him distress. Therefore, it was not morally acceptable to make that post without his agreement.
